title: Measuring delivery

story: It is the first week of December, and the head of R&D asks the question this whole project exists to answer: is Nova helping? Someone has a number ready. "We merged 31% more pull requests in November than in September." It sounds good for about ten seconds. Then the questions come. Were the PRs smaller? Did more of them break something after the merge? And is September a fair comparison, with the holidays in it?

A second person asks for a list of the slowest reviewers, "just to see". Nobody in the room can answer any of this well, and the list of reviewers is the most dangerous request of all, because a number about one person quickly becomes a ranking, and people start working for the ranking instead of the product.
hook.question: How do we measure whether delivery got better, in a way that is honest, comparable over time, and impossible to turn into a ranking of people?

read.h: Measure from events you already have
p: We do not ask anyone how fast reviews feel. GitHub already records every pull request's timeline: when it was opened, when a draft was marked ready, when each review arrived and who wrote it. A nightly job reads that timeline and computes a few delivery metrics from it. The ideas come from DORA, a long-running research programme on software delivery, whose best-known metrics are lead time and change failure rate. We adapt them to the data we have.

Take review wait, the time a PR waits for its first human review. RH-1234's PR was opened as a draft at 09:00 and marked ready at 10:00. Byte, our review agent, reviewed it at 10:20. Dana, a teammate, reviewed it at 14:00. The wait is 4 hours: the clock starts when the PR asks for review, so the draft hour does not count, and it stops at the first review by a person who is not the author, so Byte's review does not count either. The function below says exactly that, and it returns undefined, not 0, for a PR nobody has reviewed yet, because a missing review is not a fast one.

The other metrics have the same shape. Lead time runs from a PR's first commit to its merge. A change failed when a revert, a hotfix or a bug fix touched the same lines within 14 days of the merge. Red-main hours count how long fcp's main branch had a failing required test job, with overlapping failures counted once.

notes.text: A draft starts the clock when it becomes ready; a PR opened as ready starts it at creation.
Two filters: a person, not a bot such as Byte, and not the author.
No human review yet means no value. The weekly step leaves it out instead of counting a zero.

read.h: One number per team per week, with its count
p: One PR's wait says little. The job groups a week's PRs by team and turns each group into three numbers. The median is the middle value: half the PRs waited less, half waited more. The p85 is the value 85 out of 100 PRs stayed under, so it shows the slow tail, like the p95 of call times in the earlier lesson about Prometheus metrics. The count says how many PRs the numbers come from.

Why not the average? In the lab's week the frontend team's waits are 4, 1.5 and 48 hours, because one PR waited over a weekend. The mean is 17.8 hours, a wait no PR actually had. The median is 4, the typical PR, and the p85 of 48 shows the bad one separately. The count of 3 is the honest part: with about 25 engineers, one week is a small sample, and a reader who sees n = 3 knows not to panic about a single week.

Notice what the output does not contain: a login. Agent PRs count for the team of the person who requested them, a team with fewer than 3 people is reported as "other", and no series anywhere carries a person's name. That answers the second question from the meeting. A per-person number turns into a ranking, and a ranking changes behaviour in the wrong direction: people approve quickly to look fast, which makes the real metric worse.

notes.text: teamOf is passed in, so a test can use a fixed map instead of the real team list.
Map.groupBy (Node 21 and later) builds one list of PRs per team.
The count is always written, even when there are too few PRs for a median.
A median of one value is just that value, so the job writes no median below two.
One metric name with a q label, so one panel can draw p50 and p85 with the legend {{q}}.

read.h: Compared to what, and at what price
p: A number on its own cannot answer "is it helping", because it has nothing to be compared with. So before any agent opened a PR, the job was run once over the 12 weeks before October and the results were written under separate names, delivery_baseline_*. That is the baseline: what normal looked like before. Every delivery panel draws it as a flat reference line, so December's review wait is read as "above or below how we used to work", not as a number in the air. The job keeps each night's raw pull from GitHub too, so when someone finds a mistake in a formula, every week can be computed again without calling the API.

The second guard is the counterweight. Some numbers reward the wrong thing when they stand alone. Merged PRs per week, often called throughput, goes up just as nicely when the PRs are tiny or when they break things. So merged PRs is never shown without the change failure rate beside it, in the same panel. And metrics that only exist since agents started, such as the merge rate of agent PRs, begin as "no data", not 0, because a zero before the first agent PR would draw a drop that never happened.

deeper.h: Go deeper: three lenses on AI
p: DX, a company that researches developer productivity, suggests reading AI's effect through three lenses at once. Utilization: are people and agents using it, for example weekly users of Claude Code and the share of PRs with AI help? Impact: did delivery change, with change failure next to throughput? Cost: what did it take, in total and per engineer? Each lens alone tells a misleading story. Use can rise while impact falls, and impact can rise at a price nobody would choose.

Measured numbers also need people's view next to them. Studies have found developers who felt faster with AI tools while the measured numbers said they were slower. That is why our October survey asks about time lost as well as time saved, and why its answers are read next to the delivery metrics, never instead of them.

lab.title: Turn a week of pull requests into team numbers
needs: Node 22.18 or later (it runs TypeScript files directly)
No API keys, no Docker: the PRs are a fixture file
lab.goal: Compute review wait from PR timelines, group a week into team-level medians, p85s and counts, test it with node:test, and print the lines the nightly job would push.

guess.q: This week the frontend team's review waits were 4, 1.5 and 48 hours. The job reports the median and the p85. What does it report as the frontend's p50?

options.why: That is the mean. One weekend wait pulls it far above every other PR, which is exactly why the job does not use it.
Sorted, the waits are 1.5, 4 and 48, and the middle one is 4. The 48-hour wait appears in the p85 instead.
That is the slowest PR, which is the p85 here. The p50 is the middle value.

lab.build: Leadership wants to know whether agent PRs wait longer for review than human ones, which the dashboard shows as two cohorts. Add a cohort label to every point: "agent" when the PR's author is a Bot, "human" otherwise. Group by team and cohort together, for example with the key `${teamOf(pr)}|${cohort}`, and keep the rule that a median needs at least two PRs. Run node src/print.ts. You should see a count of 1 for the frontend's agent cohort and no median for it, a frontend human p50 of 24.75 from just two PRs, and the backend unchanged apart from the new label. Then fix the third test so it passes with the new labels, and say in one sentence why the count matters more than ever once the groups are smaller.

check.q: A PR was marked ready at 10:00, Byte reviewed it at 10:20, the author answered with a review comment at 11:00, and a teammate reviewed it at 13:00. What is its review wait?

options.why: Byte is a bot. We measure how long a PR waits for a person.
The author's own review does not count; nobody waits for themselves.
From ready at 10:00 to the first review by a person who is not the author, at 13:00.

check.q: Someone asks to add a reviewer label to delivery_review_wait_hours, "so we can help the slow ones". What is the problem?

options.text: A per-person number turns into a ranking, and people then work for the ranking, for example by approving quickly without reading
options.why: That is why every series is team level, small teams fold into "other", and no dashboard has a person dropdown.

options.text: VictoriaMetrics cannot store a label with a person's name
options.why: It could store it. The reason is what the number does to people, not a technical limit.

options.text: There is no problem, as long as only managers can see the dashboard
options.why: Who sees it does not change what it does: a ranking still changes behaviour, and the data still describes one person.

check.q: November shows 31% more merged PRs than the baseline. Which extra fact would most change how you read that?

options.text: The total number of commits in November
options.why: That is another throughput number. It moves with merged PRs and says nothing about quality.

options.text: That the delivery dashboard was redesigned in November
options.why: The dashboard draws the numbers; changing its look does not change them.

options.text: That the change failure rate doubled over the same weeks
options.why: More merges with twice the breakage is not better delivery. That is why throughput always sits next to its counterweight.

p: The nightly delivery-metrics job is a TypeScript workspace, ai-agents/metrics, run by a GitHub Actions workflow at 02:20 UTC. It reads fcp's PRs through GitHub's GraphQL API with a separate read-only GitHub App, one week per search because a search stops at 1,000 results, adds Jira tickets for project RH and the required unit-test runs on main, and stores each day's raw pull as an artifact. It computes the metrics with p50, p85 and counts per team and week, folds teams under 3 people into "other", and pushes the lines with timestamps to VictoriaMetrics, as the lesson about Prometheus metrics showed. The baseline came from one run of delivery-metrics backfill --weeks 12 --until 2026-09-30, checked by hand against GitHub on three numbers.

Agent PRs count for the requester's team, and agent-only metrics (agent PR merge rate, human rework, CI auto-fix success) start as no data. Byte's addressed and wrong-finding rates and the runtime's stuck-loop and clean-ending counts are copied into the same delivery_ names, seventeen series in all, and the three lenses are written as delivery_lens_* series and shown in a row at the top of the delivery dashboard. How to count human-equivalent hours of agent work is still a decision for leadership; the proposal is the estimate in Nova's approved plan.

tickets.why: The job itself: the GraphQL pull, one week per query, the push with timestamps and the 02:20 workflow.
Jira tickets and CI runs on main, with red-main hours counted once for overlapping failures.
Review wait, lead time, change failure and the weekly team points, plus the 12-week baseline.
The three lenses, utilization, impact and cost, computed from the same inputs.
The October survey, team level only, read next to the measured numbers.

words.plain: Hours from a PR asking for review (ready, or opened if never a draft) to the first review by a person other than the author.
The middle value: half the PRs waited less, half waited more. One extreme value barely moves it.
The value 85 out of 100 PRs stayed at or under. It shows the slow tail.
A merged PR whose lines a revert, hotfix or bug fix touched within 14 days.
The same metrics for the 12 weeks before agents started, drawn as a reference line on every panel.

review.q: Define review wait precisely enough that two people would compute the same number.
review.a: From ready for review (or opening, if the PR was never a draft) to the first review whose author is a User and not the PR's author. No such review means no value, not zero.

review.q: Why does each weekly point come with a count, and what should a reader do when n is 3?
review.a: Weekly samples are small, so the count says how much the median can be trusted. With n = 3, watch the trend over several weeks and against the baseline instead of reacting to one week.

review.q: Name the two guards that keep a delivery number honest, besides team level only.
review.a: A baseline from before the change, drawn on every panel, and a counterweight: throughput only next to change failure.

remember: Compute delivery from events you already have, one team-level median, p85 and count per week, and read it only against its baseline and next to its counterweight.
